opus-5.5.text:
I think Sergey is really one of the best at this, and it's something I only appreciated after working with him closely.

When most of us write a paper, especially early in a PhD, we tend to write it in the order we did the work. We tried this, it didn't work, we added that, here are the results. Sergey almost never thinks that way. Before the experiments are even finished, he's already asking: what is the one sentence someone should remember from this paper? What problem does it reframe, and why should someone outside our immediate subfield care?

The introduction is where you see it most. He'll often rewrite it so it starts from a much bigger question, something about how robots should learn, or what's actually blocking generalization, and then narrow down step by step until your method feels like the natural, almost inevitable answer. By the time the reader reaches the technical section, they already believe the idea should work, and the experiments become confirmation rather than persuasion.

He's also very disciplined about cutting. If something is technically interesting but doesn't serve the main story, it goes to the appendix, even if you spent two months on it. That's painful as a student, but the paper becomes much clearer.

And he's incredibly fast. You send him a draft at night, and the next morning there's a restructured version where the logic just flows. I think part of it is that he has thought about the big picture of the field for so long that he can immediately place any piece of work within it. So the storytelling isn't really a writing trick. It comes from having a clear view of where the field is going and where your paper fits into that.

fable-5.1.text:
Sergey is, honestly, one of the best people I've ever seen at this. And I think it's underrated how much of a skill it is, because a lot of people assume that a paper is just the experiments plus some words around them. For Sergey, the story comes first.

What I mean is, when you bring him a result, the first thing he does isn't look at the numbers. He asks, what is the one sentence? If you can't say in one sentence what this paper is about and why someone should care, he'll keep pushing until you can. And very often that process changes the paper. You realize the interesting thing isn't the thing you set out to show, it's some side observation you were going to put in the appendix. He has a very good nose for that.

The second thing is that he writes the intro like he's arguing with a skeptical reader. Every paragraph is answering a "so what" or a "but why not just do X." He'll literally say, okay, a reviewer reads this sentence, what's the objection, and then the next sentence should address it. So by the time you get to the method, the reader already feels like the method is the obvious thing to do. That's the trick, right? Make the idea feel inevitable rather than clever.

And he's very disciplined about not overclaiming. I think people sometimes confuse storytelling with hype, and it's actually the opposite with him. The story is sharper precisely because it's narrow. He'd rather say "we show this works in this regime and here's why" than "this is a general solution." Funny enough, that makes the papers age better.

The thing I took away personally, and I still do this, is I write the abstract before I run the big experiments. Not because I know the result, but because if I can't write an abstract that I'd be excited to read, the experiments probably aren't worth running yet. I got that directly from him. He'd say, if the story only works if the numbers come out a certain way, you don't have a story, you have a gamble.

So yeah, I'd say he treats the paper as the actual research artifact, not the code or the plots. The plots are evidence for the story. And I think that's why so many of his papers get read and remembered, even the ones where the method itself got superseded pretty quickly.

sol-6.1.text: I think the strength of storytelling in an academic paper is making the reader understand why each step matters. You start with a question, explain why the obvious approaches don’t quite resolve it, and then show how the main idea moves things forward. That’s the lens I’d use to assess Sergey’s writing: does the story clarify the reasoning, and does the evidence support the story?
